newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Tranz Rail eyeing Australian rail - Small.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Tranz Rail eyeing Australian rail - Small.

text.p: New Zealand's Tranz Rail is keen to buy part of Australian rail assets about to be privatised, Managing Director Francis Small said on Friday.
"The fact of the matter is Australia is close to us. There is an opportunity there but how we approach it and how we structure it I can't tell yet," he said in an interview.
"Going to Australia is one way of growing the business and we have to keep all our options open."
The Australian government said on Sunday it would sell Australian National (AN) and its 40 percent stake in National Rail Corp which operates inter-state freight services.
Small said there were many issues yet to be considered about how Australia would sell the assets.
Should Tranz Rail bid, it would be likely do so in conjuction with U.S. majority shareholder, Wisconsin Central, which has been an aggressive acquirer of privatised railroads such as Tranz Rail.
Small said Tranz Rail could be interested in all or any one of the five parts of AN but would not bid for the sake of it.
"If by ownership we can add value then clearly we are in the business of expanding where we have core competency."
Tranz Rail would most likely be lining up against Australian transport giant TNT Ltd, National Rail, Howard Smith Ltd, A Goninan and Co and Bradken of Australian National Industries Ltd among others.
AN has assets officially valued at about A$1.2 billion but Canberra has said it will spend about A$2 billion preparing it for sale including assuming A$1 billion of debts.
Small said AN would not be too big a bite for Tranz Rail at around three-quarters Tranz Rail's size.
Although a mature business in New Zealand, Tranz Rail's growth will not be limited to outside the country.

"There are three growth opportunities -- organic growth of traditional businesses, there's the specific growth opportunities of forestry and coal and then there is the emergence of new businesses -- milk, refuse and other commodities we have not been involved in more strongly... as well as what we might do offshore."
Chief Financial Officer Ron Russ said that despite a strong New Zealand dollar and slowing economic growth, volumes in the freight export sector had been encouraging.
"Domestically, the retail side had slowed up, but other parts, particularly on the export side, good volumes are being moved," he said.

He expects profit trends of the first quarter to continue through the year. Earlier this month Tranz Rail reported a one percent rise in operating profit to NZ$18.0 million and a 60 percent in net profit to $9.4 million for the quarter.
"I think we are going to see a continuation of those kind of trends in the near term," Russ said.

He sees profit growth coming from a combination of cost cutting and revenue growth. Growth in key freight segments -- forestry, coal and dairy products would underpin "better than average top line growth".

He estimated Tranz Rail had boosted freight market share from 18 percent five years ago and 20 percent two years ago by a couple of percentage points but Tranz Rail does not yet have the data to verify it.
"We believe we have grown our market share in that inter-regional segment," he said.

Tranz Rail's large capital expenditure programme -- NZ$600 million over ten years mainly to replace inter island ferries and the port terminals -- would be funded by either debt or equity, but more likely debt at this stage, he said.
Local analysts have been cool on Tranz Rail, saying it is overvalued with a high P/E ratio at 16. Most interest in the stock has come from the U.S. where it is also listed.

However, Russ said railroad stocks are enjoying a renaissance in the U.S. and the rise in the share price to NZ$8.40 from its $6.95 listing price in June suggests the U.S. analysts may have made a better call.
